Dear Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and Members of the Committee on
Health and Human Services:
My name is Kevin Voyvodich and I am an attorney at Disability Rights Maine
Maine's designated protection and advocacy agency for individuals with disabilities.
I am here today to testify in support of LD 831.
DRM has become aware of this important issue for individuals held involuntarily in
psychiatric hospitals who have had their vehicle towed during the mental health crisis
that lead to the hospitalization. Currently Maine law allows for vehicles towed under certain circumstances to be considered abandoned under the law if certain paperwork and timelines requirements are met by a towing company.` This process does not account for the realities faced by people experiencing a psychiatric crisis. For
individuals who are court-committed to a psychiatric hospital, the timeframe to
reclaim a vehicle is often too short, and the fees charged by towing companies can be
prohibitively expensive.
This bill addresses that problem by extending the window for reclaiming a towed
vehicle to 120 days. This timeframe mirrors the maximum duration someone can be
held under an initial involuntary psychiatric commitment? It also reflects the fact that
I Sec 29-A M.R.S. �� 1851-1856 2 34-B M.R.S. � 3864

many individuals spend days or even weeks in emergency rooms before being transferred to a psychiatric facility, at which point the involuntary legal process begins.
Further this bill reduces the maximum amount an individual can be required to pay, from $1,500 to $600 for the first thirty days of storage fees. Many individuals that I have worked with who are in the hospital have limited funds and this fee reduction better allows them to either cover the cost fully using their own funds or apply for any
emergency funding available from the state. This bill also protects the individual's privacy because it will only apply if the person gives permission to share that they are involuntarily hospitalized, which then allows them to obtain the expanded timeline and lower cost.
I will end with two examples of how challenging this can be for an individual. In one
situation, one of our state hospital-based advocates and I worked with an individual to retrieve their vehicle. By the time all was said and done, the individual was able to retrieve their vehicle only after obtaining over $2,000.00 in state funds to do so. If
DRM had not intervened, the individual could have lost title to their vehicle, which
they still owed money on. In another example, an individual reached out to one of our
state hospital advocates about their car, but unfortunately the vehicle title had already been transferred to the towing company and the car had been sold.
The examples above clearly show how high the financial cost can be for the individual. Even worse, in some cases when the person finally is in a place to look to
retrieve their vehicle, it might already be gone. This bill simply tries to provide a
person, held involuntarily in mental health crisis, more of a chance to retain their vehicle. Once a person is ready for hospital discharge after receiving treatment, they should not be leaving without vital access to the vehicle that they owned when they
entered the hospital.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Kevin D. Voyvodich
Managing Attorney

LD 831 An Act Regarding Abandoned Vehicles Due to Involuntary Psychiatric Hospitalization
Good afternoon, Senator lngwersen, Representative Meyer and my fellow distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services. As you know, my name is Marianne Moore. l proudly represent Senate District 6 which includes all of
Washington County and 16 Communities in Eastern Hancock County as well.
I'm here to introduce LD984 -- An Act Regarding Abandoned Vehicles Due to Involuntary
Psychiatric Hospitalization.
Last fall l was contacted by Disability Rights Maine (DRM) and asked if l would be willing to submit this bill addressing an issue that is being seen in hospitals, mostly Riverview, due to the
longer stays being experienced. DRM and the State Office of Behavioral Health (OBH) have
become more aware of a small but very important issue that happens to some individuals who
have a vehicle but end up in crisis and are hospitalized. Often if an individual shows up to an
ER and their car is in the parking lot or even somewhere else when a crisis happens, tow
companies get called and often if a person in crisis doesn't think of the issue (l can totally
relate as to when I have been in crisis), towing companies have a lot of leeway to take ownership of the vehicle, which may be someone's only possession, etc. if no one thinks to
make a plan to help the person get their car put somewhere safe. DRM has worked with
several individuals that have had this happen and some of the vehicles are not just beat up
cars either. OBH has helped with wrap around funds to save people's cars. The general concept of this bill is to have a few guardrails in place when this happens.
To give you a brief idea of how the whole "Abandoned Auto" Statute works... After a vehicle
has been towed and declared "Abandoned" either in a parking lot or on a public roadway,
after 14 days the towing company notifies the Secretary of State (SOS) who in turn sends a letter to the owner giving them 14 days to respond or take action. When there is no response,
the ownership of the vehicle goes to the towing company. In the case of involuntary/voluntary admission to psychiatric hospitals due to a medical crisis, the vehicle
may remain with the towing company for an extended period of time and ultimately assigned

Shenna Bellows, Secretary of State Department of the Secretary of State, Bureau of Motor Vehicles
March 25, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and
Human Services, my name is Shenna Bellows. I am the Secretary of State and I reside in Manchester. I am providing testimony Neither for Nor Against L.D. 831 "An Act Regarding Abandoned Vehicles Due
to Involuntary Psychiatric Hospitalization."
The towing industry is largely unregulated and Mainers -- whether involuntarily hospitalized or not -
have raised serious consumer protection concerns. In order to look for a path forward for this industry that better protects Maine vehicle owners, the Bureau of Motor Vehicles is working with Senator Nangle on a bill to call for a working group to bring together industry, law enforcement, consumer protection advocates, and financial institutions to discuss this very issue. The issues raised in L.D. 831 would fit very well in that discussion, and Senator Nangle has agreed it should be a topic of discussion for the working group.
In addition to our suggestion that inclusion of this topic in a study group as the best and most
comprehensive path forward, we have concerns with the bill as written. Enactment of this bill would
result in the BMV's Titles Division receiving notice of someone's hospitalization. We have concerns for
the sharing of private medical information with a division which normally would not receive information about a customers' health.
For these reasons, we think that the working group is the right path forward for this issue at this time.
Perhaps the recommended resolution for this specific population and issue will be the one proposed in
L.D. 831, but we think it should be discussed more robustly with all relevant interested parties before
advancing this bill at this time.
Thank you for your time today and I will be happy to answer any questions.

Testimony of Jason Goodrich
Regarding LD 831 - An Act Regarding Abandoned Vehicles Due to Involuntary Psychiatric Hospitalization
Members of the Health and Human Committee:
My name is Jason Goodrich, and I am corresponding today to express my strong support for LD 831. I come to you as someone who has worked with individuals experiencing crisis, homelessness, and behavioral health concerns, and I ask you to consider a simple truth: when any of us are in trouble, the thing we most often ask for is "just a little more time."
Think about the last time you faced hardship. Maybe you lost a job, had a health scare, or found yourself overwhelmed by life's circumstances. When that moment came, if you needed help, chances are you asked for just a little more time to figure things out--time to pay that bill, to decide, to get back on your feet.
Now imagine you are in crisis--not just struggling, but in such distress that the state deems it necessary to hospitalize you involuntarily - to reduce your rights as a citizen. Your world is already spinning. And while you are locked away, without any ability to intervene, the clock is ticking on your only means of transportation--your car, parked somewhere, waiting to be towed and claimed as abandoned.
For many, a vehicle is more than just a car. It's independence. It's stability. Sometimes it's even housing! It's the last thing We have left after losing jobs, homes, or relationships. It represents the hope that, when we walk out of the hospital doors, we have something left to rebuild with.
LD 831 recognizes this reality. It gives people that extra time--120 days--before their vehicle is considered abandoned. That may not seem like much, but when someone is returning from hospitalization, those extra days can be the difference between recovery and relapse, between work and unemployment, between stability and homelessness.
This bill isn't about handouts--it's about fairness and dignity. It's about recognizing that when people are at their lowest, we don't need to take away one more thing. We need to give them what all of us, at some point, have needed: just a little more time.
I urge you to support LD 831 and help ensure that behavioral health crisis do not become an irreversible downward spiral for any of us.
Thank you. Jason Goodrich
